Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Authority Presence: Police, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Priya had been on her hands and knees in the ground-floor showroom, smoothing out a bolt of indigo silk, when the heavy glass doors opened without warning. Two officers stepped into the narrow aisle, their navy jackets stiff with epaulets, their presence immediately shifting the air in the room. She remembered the sharp grit of the unpolished terrazzo floor grinding into her palms, the way the space felt suddenly constricted. She knew what was happening, yet when she tried to reconstruct it later, the words dissolved in her mouth. There were stretches of time that simply vanished, replaced by sudden, disconnected flashes: a radio crackling, the heavy thud of boots on concrete, the way the fluorescent light caught the silver buttons on their uniforms. She tried to piece them together, to find the sequence, but the gaps remained, solid and impenetrable, leaving her with fragments that refused to align. In the weeks that followed, Priya stopped answering the door for unexpected visitors. She told herself she was buried in a new renovation, but the truth was heavier. Every time a delivery driver’s dark coat brushed past her studio window, her shoulders locked. She stopped taking clients to her ground-floor space. The coarse terrazzo now felt like a live wire under her shoes, and she found herself booking every meeting upstairs or at a quiet café, where the flooring was smooth and familiar. Over the months, the habits hardened. She declined a lucrative commercial contract after noticing the developer’s security staff wore identical uniforms. She stopped updating her design portfolio. She would trace the edges of her sketchbooks, looking for a narrative that would finally make sense, but the pages only held measurements and fabric codes, nothing that could explain the silence that followed. What frightened Priya most was the suddenness of her own reactions. She could not deal with even the slightest upset; a dropped file folder would send her breath into shallow, rapid pulls, her hands trembling until she forced herself to sit. She was certain that her body kept reacting as if she were still standing on that floor, even when her kitchen tiles were cool and steady under her feet. The fear of another surprise was a quiet but constant companion. She had come to believe that nothing good could happen to her anymore, that the windows of opportunity had simply closed. At seventy-three, widowed for five years, she stopped making plans beyond the next season. The breaking point came three months ago, during a site walk-through at a new residential complex. A uniformed guard stepped into her line of sight, and Priya’s vision narrowed to that specific texture of woven twill on his sleeve. She had to leave the building, leaving her measuring tape and client notes on a folding table. She sat in her car for an hour, unable to steady her pulse, realizing she could no longer pretend the studio was safe. She called the clinic on a Tuesday morning, her voice barely above a whisper. She was not sure what she would find here, but she hoped, fiercely, for a way to walk into a room without bracing for a door to open.
